name: Pulse-point fragrance application

lead: Pulse points are places where blood vessels run close to the skin, such as the wrists, sides of the neck, behind the ears and inner elbows. Fragrance makers and enthusiasts apply scent there because the skin is warm, which is said to help the fragrance diffuse and last.

The appearance payoff is indirect: scent is part of the overall impression a person makes alongside grooming and style. Placement is a way to adjust how strongly a scent projects, and no clinical study has tested pulse-point placement as a looks intervention.

paras: People typically apply fragrance to clean, dry or lightly moisturised skin on a few spots, such as the neck, chest and wrists, rather than only to clothes. Several perfumers advise patting rather than rubbing the wrists together, which they say dulls the top notes. Lighter concentrations such as colognes are usually reapplied during the day, while stronger ones are used more sparingly.

Fragrance is a common allergen and can cause contact irritation, and the skin of the neck is sensitive. Experts advise keeping fragrance away from the eyes and delicate skin, and people with sensitive or eczema-prone skin are told to check with a dermatologist. Strong scents may bother others in shared spaces, and alcohol-based perfumes can stain silk and light fabrics.

chain: Scent projects and lasts through the day
Pleasant smell adds to overall impression
angle.text: Users apply fragrance to warm spots so the scent is noticeable at conversational distance and holds up through the day. It supplements grooming and clothing as part of how someone comes across.

lead: Pulse-point fragrance application is the habit of applying perfume or cologne to places where the skin is warm, typically the wrists, sides of the neck, behind the ears, inner elbows and behind the knees. The usual explanation is that body heat helps the scent develop and spread, so the fragrance acts as a natural diffuser [1][2][3].

As a grooming step, it supports how a person comes across: a pleasant smell sits alongside clothing, skin and hair as part of the overall impression. Placement is used to control how far a scent carries (projection) and how long it lasts (longevity), and fragrance communities and perfumers give detailed advice on both [2][3][1].
Perfumers disagree on some details, notably whether rubbing the wrists together after spraying changes how the scent opens. No clinical study has examined pulse-point placement.
infobox: Wrists, sides of neck, behind ears, inner elbows, behind knees [1][3]
Cologne 2-3%, eau de toilette 5-15%, eau de parfum 15-20%, parfum 15-30% [4]

paras: Traditionally, pure perfume is applied to pulse points behind the ears, at the nape, on the wrists, elbows and knees so body heat releases the scent [4]. Perfumers describe warm skin as a natural diffuser that starts the scent's unfolding [3][1]. Chemist and former Chanel fragrance expert Matthew Milèo says the skin's warmth starts the 'unraveling process' of a perfume [3].

How long a scent lasts depends on its concentration and on the wearer. Reference estimates put cologne at roughly two hours, eau de toilette at two to four hours and perfume at up to six to eight, with diet, medication and skin dryness all playing a part [4]. Perfumer Darryl Do adds that temperature, humidity and skin moisture affect longevity, and that a midday refresh is acceptable [2].

Advice from fragrance professionals commonly lists the wrists, sides of the neck, chest, inner elbows, behind the ears and behind the knees [3][1]. Matt Moore, founder of EastWest Bottlers, recommends a few dabs or a single spritz at these points [1]. Savannah Britt of The Fragrance Affair favours a more generous spread across the body and suggests applying perfume oils to the wrists and neck because oils evaporate less readily [1].

subs.h: Skin preparation and the rubbing question
paras: Several experts say fragrance holds better on hydrated skin: Melina Polly of Henry Rose recommends spraying after a shower or over lotion [3], and a Glamour feature makes the same suggestion [2]. Perfumers quoted by Glamour and Yahoo advise patting rather than rubbing the wrists together, saying friction weakens the top notes [3][2]. Moore similarly recommends letting the fragrance dry on the skin [1].

Some experts spray washable fabrics, since cloth holds part of a scent, though it can smell more powdery than on skin [3]. Perfume oils can stain silk and light fabrics [3][2]. Alcohol-based perfumes can dry hair, so water-based scents are used there instead [3].

Scent is often listed with grooming basics in style-focused communities, alongside skincare, haircare and clothing. Discussions centre on which areas to use, how many sprays, and how a given concentration behaves on skin. Social-media fragrance enthusiasts have also circulated techniques for 'catching' a cologne, and opinions differ on details such as rubbing the wrists [2].

Fragrance is a common allergen, and people with sensitive or eczema-prone skin are advised to consult a dermatologist before applying it [3]. Britt advises keeping fragrance away from the eyes and intimate areas, where delicate skin is sensitive to alcohol and fragrance compounds [1]. Perfumer Darryl Do likewise advises keeping it off the face, eyes and mouth [2]. If too much has been applied, Moore suggests wiping the skin gently with a damp warm cloth [1].

timeline.event: Eau de cologne is first recorded [4].
Guerlain's Jicky becomes the first fragrance labelled 'parfum' [4].
Eau de parfum emerges, becoming popular in the 1980s [4].
